# @fathym/ioc: the complete documentation

> Dependency injection for modern TypeScript. No decorators. No metadata. Async from the ground up.

Every page of the docs in reading order, then the example programs. Every TypeScript block and example here is type-checked and run in CI against this version. The index is [llms.txt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/llms.txt).

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/README.md

# @fathym/ioc

### Dependency injection for modern TypeScript. No decorators. No metadata. Async from the ground up.

[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@fathym/ioc)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fathym/ioc)
[![JSR](https://jsr.io/badges/@fathym/ioc)](https://jsr.io/@fathym/ioc)
[![JSR Score](https://jsr.io/badges/@fathym/ioc/score)](https://jsr.io/@fathym/ioc/score)
[![Build](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/actions/workflows/build.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/actions/workflows/build.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/LICENSE)

Most TypeScript DI containers were built for a world of `experimentalDecorators` and
`reflect-metadata`. They break under esbuild, Vite and Vitest, they resolve synchronously while
your database connects asynchronously, and they tell you about a missing dependency when the first
request hits it.

**@fathym/ioc is built for how TypeScript apps are written today.** Plain classes. Typed keys.
Async factories that just work. Wiring mistakes caught by the compiler, and the rest caught at
startup. Clean shutdown when you're done. It runs on Deno, Node.js and Bun, in about 6 KB gzipped,
with zero dependencies.

```ts
import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

interface Mailer {
  send(to: string, body: string): Promise<void>;
}

class Db {
  static async connect(url: string) {
    return new Db(url); // open your real connection pool here
  }

  constructor(public url: string) {}

  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    console.log('db closed');
  }
}

class Signup {
  constructor(private db: Db, private mailer: Mailer) {}

  async register(email: string) {
    await this.mailer.send(email, `Welcome! (saved to ${this.db.url})`);
  }
}

const $Mailer = IoCToken<Mailer>('app/Mailer');

{
  await using ioc = new IoCContainer()
    .RegisterFactory(Db, () => Db.connect('postgres://localhost/app')) // async, built once
    .RegisterValue($Mailer, { send: async (to, body) => console.log(`to ${to}: ${body}`) })
    .RegisterClass(Signup, { Deps: [Db, $Mailer] }); // checked against the constructor

  ioc.Validate(); // every wiring mistake, reported before anything runs

  const signup = await ioc.Resolve(Signup); // typed as Signup

  await signup.register('ada@example.com'); // to ada@example.com: Welcome! (saved to …)
} // db closed: whatever the container built is disposed, in reverse order
```

## Why teams pick it

- **🧩 No decorators, no metadata, no build step.** Your classes stay plain TypeScript. Nothing
  depends on `emitDecoratorMetadata`, so it works the same under esbuild, Vite, tsx, Vitest, Deno,
  Node.js and Bun.
- **🛡️ Mistakes caught by the compiler.** `Deps` is checked against your constructor, in order
  and by type. Turn on `Typed()` and using a service before it's registered won't compile.
- **🔍 The rest caught at startup.** `Validate()` lists every missing dependency, cycle and
  lifetime mistake in one go, without building anything. Put it in one test and wiring bugs never
  reach production.
- **⚡ Async is first-class.** Factories can be `async`. Concurrent requests share one build, and a
  connection that fails is retried on the next resolve instead of being cached as broken.
- **🧹 Clean shutdown, built in.** One scope per request with `await using`. Everything the
  container built is disposed in reverse order. Modules start in dependency order and stop in
  reverse, so your server drains before your database closes.
- **🧪 Easy to test.** `Override()` swaps any service for a fake and hands you a restore
  function. Test against the real wiring, not a hand-built copy of it.
- **📖 Errors that explain themselves.** Every error has a stable code and an
  [entry in the catalog](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/reference/errors.md) with
  the cause and the fix.

## See it in action

**A scope per request,** cleaned up when the request ends:

```ts
import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

const $Request = IoCToken<{ path: string }>('app/Request');

class RequestContext {
  public id = crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8);
}

class Handler {
  constructor(private req: { path: string }, private ctx: RequestContext) {}

  handle() {
    return `${this.ctx.id} handled ${this.req.path}`;
  }
}

const app = new IoCContainer()
  .RegisterClass(RequestContext, { Lifetime: 'scoped' }) // one per request
  .RegisterClass(Handler, { Deps: [$Request, RequestContext], Lifetime: 'transient' });

for (const path of ['/notes', '/users']) {
  await using scope = app.CreateScope().RegisterValue($Request, { path });

  console.log((await scope.Resolve(Handler)).handle()); // 3f9c1a2b handled /notes …
}
```

**A constructor change the wiring didn't follow** doesn't compile:

```ts
import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class Db {}
class Cache {}

class Repo {
  constructor(public db: Db, public cache: Cache) {} // gained a Cache parameter
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer().RegisterClass(Db).RegisterClass(Cache);

ioc.RegisterClass(Repo, {
  // @ts-expect-error Source has 1 element(s) but target requires 2.
  Deps: [Db],
});
```

**Modules with a lifecycle,** started in order and stopped in reverse:

```ts
import { DefineModule, IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

const Database = DefineModule({
  Name: 'Database',
  Register: (ioc) => ioc,
  OnStart: () => console.log('database connected'),
  OnStop: () => console.log('database closed'),
});

const Api = DefineModule({
  Name: 'Api',
  Requires: [Database], // started after Database, stopped before it
  Register: (ioc) => ioc,
  OnStart: () => console.log('api listening'),
  OnStop: () => console.log('api drained'),
});

{
  await using app = new IoCContainer().Use(Api);

  await app.Start(); // database connected, api listening
} // api drained, database closed
```

## How it compares

|                                                        | @fathym/ioc | InversifyJS | tsyringe | awilix  | NestJS |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | :---------: | :---------: | :------: | :-----: | :----: |
| No decorators or `reflect-metadata`                    |      ✓      |      ~      |    ✗     |    ✓    |   ✗    |
| A wrong dependency fails to compile †                  |      ✓      |      ~      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   ✗    |
| An async dependency is injected ready, not a promise † |      ✓      |      ✓      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   ✓    |
| A failed async build is retried, not cached †          |      ✓      |      ✗      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   –    |
| Disposes a service before its dependencies †           |      ✓      |      ✗      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   –    |
| A missing dependency is found at startup †             |      ✓      |      ✗      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   ✓    |
| Modules with start/stop lifecycle                      |      ✓      |      ~      |    ✗     |    ✗    |   ✓    |
| Standalone library, not a framework                    |      ✓      |      ✓      |    ✓     |    ✓    |   ✗    |
| Synchronous resolve                                    |      ✗      |      ✓      |    ✓     |    ✓    |   ✓    |
| Minified + gzipped                                     | **6.1 KB**  |   24.7 KB   | 11.0 KB  | 30.1 KB | 141 KB |
| Runtime dependencies                                   |    **0**    |    6 + 1    |  1 + 1   |   18    | 18 + 2 |

✓ yes · ~ partly · ✗ no · – not measured. **Rows marked † are measured, not taken from docs:**
`deno task compare` runs the same scenarios and benchmarks against each library at pinned versions
(InversifyJS 8.2, tsyringe 4.10, awilix 13.0) and writes the
[comparison page](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/reference/comparison.md), with the
code for every cell. InversifyJS checks dependencies at compile time with `toResolvedValue`, not
with `@inject` decorators, and loads `reflect-metadata` itself. NestJS cells come from its
documentation. On raw speed the synchronous containers win: a resolve here takes about 1 µs
against 50–200 ns; the comparison page has the numbers.

Sizes are each whole library bundled with its required polyfill and measured with
`deno task size --compare` (NestJS 12.3 core and common). Dependencies count indirect ones;
"+ 1" is `reflect-metadata`, and NestJS's "+ 2" adds rxjs. awilix's browser build leaves out file
scanning and is 3.6 KB.

Need several implementations of one interface, such as a chain of handlers or one cache per
region? Register each under a
[name](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/reference/api.md#resolveallkey) and
collect them with `ResolveAll`. A whole folder of modules registers with one call, too: see
[registering many modules](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/guides/registering-many-modules.md).

**Pick something else if** you need synchronous resolution everywhere, auto-registration by
scanning files and naming conventions (awilix does this well), property injection or bindings
chosen by tags and injection target (InversifyJS), or you're inside a framework with its own DI,
such as NestJS or Angular.

## Install

```sh
npm install @fathym/ioc      # Node.js 20+ (or pnpm add, yarn add)
bun add @fathym/ioc          # Bun
deno add jsr:@fathym/ioc     # Deno
```

TypeScript 5.4 or later. See the
[requirements](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/getting-started/installation.md#requirements).

Every code example in the docs is type-checked and run in CI, so what you read is what works. The
generated API docs are on [JSR](https://jsr.io/@fathym/ioc/doc), and AI tools can start from
[`llms.txt`](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/llms.txt).

## Built to be depended on

- **A stable 1.x API.** Breaking changes only in a major release, each with a migration guide, and
  anything deprecated keeps working for at least six months. The
  [versioning policy](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/policy.md) defines exactly what
  counts as breaking.
- **Proven, not just promised.** The
  [guarantees](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/reference/guarantees.md) list what
  the container promises about builds, disposal, startup, timeouts and `Validate()`, each linked
  to the test that proves it. CI fails if a linked test goes away, and test coverage of the source
  is 98.8% of lines and 97.1% of branches, with CI failing below 97% and 95%.
- **Measured against the alternatives.** The
  [comparison](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/reference/comparison.md) runs the
  same scenarios and benchmarks against InversifyJS, awilix and tsyringe, and you can re-run it.
- **Tested on every runtime it supports:** the full suite on Deno, and the published build on
  Node.js 20, 22 and 24 and Bun, type-checked with TypeScript 5.4 and the latest.
- **Answered:** security reports are acknowledged within 3 business days and new issues triaged
  within 5 ([maintainers](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/MAINTAINERS.md)).
- **Yours to own if you need to:** MIT, no dependencies, and about 2,700 lines including
  documentation comments.
- **Every change** is in the [changelog](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

Deciding whether to adopt it?
[Evaluating @fathym/ioc](https://github.com/fathym/ioc/blob/main/docs/evaluating.md) covers
support, the honest risks, and how to adopt it safely.

Built and maintained by [Fathym](https://github.com/fathym), whose own platform, from the CLI to
the runtime, is built on it.

example in these docs is type-checked and run in CI.

## Conventions

How these docs are written. [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md#documentation) explains how to add a
page.

- **Frontmatter on every page** in the house schema (`FrontmatterVersion`, `DocumentType`,
  `Title`, `Summary`, `Created`, `Updated`, `Owners`, `References`).
- **One idea per example.** Each example is a complete module that type-checks and runs in CI.
  Tokens are written `IoCToken<T, 'Name'>('Name')` where a typed container needs the name in the
  type, and `IoCToken<T>('Name')` otherwise.
- **1.0 as it is.** Pages describe the current API only; changes from 0.x live in the
  [migration guide](./migration/from-0.x.md) and the [changelog](../CHANGELOG.md).
- **Links are tagged by type** (_[Tutorial]_, _[How-to]_, _[Explanation]_, _[Reference]_), and
  every page ends with **What's Next**.
- **Limits are stated plainly.** No page implies a capability the container doesn't have.

# Evaluating @fathym/ioc

> **Goal:** decide whether your team should depend on `@fathym/ioc`, with the evidence in one
> place.

A dependency injection container sits under the whole application, so the question isn't only
"is the API nice" but "can we rely on it". This page answers the questions reviewers ask, and
states the risks plainly.

## At a glance

| What                     | Where it stands                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stable since             | 1.0, November 2026 (`1.0.18` was the first stable release); the 0.x line ran from 2025                                           |
| Breaking changes         | Only in a major release, with a migration guide ([policy](./policy.md#semantic-versioning))                                      |
| Behavior you can rely on | [Guarantees](./reference/guarantees.md), each linked to the test that proves it; CI fails if one is removed                      |
| Test coverage of `src/`  | 98.8% of lines, 97.1% of branches; CI fails below 97% / 95% (`deno task coverage`)                                               |
| Runtimes                 | Full suite on Deno 2; the published build on Node.js 20, 22 and 24 and Bun; TypeScript 5.4 and later                             |
| Size and dependencies    | About 6 KB minified and gzipped; no runtime dependencies                                                                         |
| Compared with others     | [The same scenarios and benchmarks](./reference/comparison.md) against InversifyJS, awilix and tsyringe                          |
| License                  | MIT                                                                                                                              |
| Maintainers              | Listed in [MAINTAINERS.md](../MAINTAINERS.md); new issues triaged within 5 business days, security reports acknowledged within 3 |

## Questions reviewers ask

- **What is the support commitment for 1.x?** The latest 1.x release gets bug and security fixes.
  Anything deprecated keeps working for at least one minor release and at least six months, and is
  removed only in a major release. Dropping a runtime version is announced a release ahead. The
  details are in the [versioning and support policy](./policy.md).
- **Are breaking changes limited to major releases?** Yes. The policy defines breaking precisely:
  exports, signatures, error codes, documented behavior (lifetimes, ordering, disposal, what
  `Validate()` reports, option defaults) and supported runtimes. Error message text is not part of
  the contract; error codes are.
- **How are security issues handled?** Privately, through GitHub security advisories, with an
  acknowledgement within three business days. See the [security policy](../SECURITY.md).
- **Is it feature-complete, and what's the roadmap?** It is intentionally small. A feature is added
  only when it fixes a bug real applications hit or replaces something they do by hand; the
  [design notes](./design/ioc-1.0.md) list what was left out and why. Expect fixes and small,
  additive minor releases, not a growing framework. Synchronous resolution of already-built
  services is the one addition under consideration.
- **Who else uses it in production?** Fathym's own platform, from its CLI to its runtime, runs on
  the 0.x line, and is moving to 1.0. Outside adoption is new. If you adopt it, tell us in an issue or a discussion; it helps everyone judge
  the same question.
- **What if the maintainers stop?** You can own it. It is MIT-licensed, has no dependencies, and is
  about 2,700 lines including its documentation comments, in one folder (`src/ioc/`). The tests
  and the docs check come with it.

## The honest risks

- **It is young.** The stable API dates from November 2026 and the user base is small, so there
  are fewer answers online than for InversifyJS, awilix or tsyringe.
- **Resolution is always asynchronous.** Every `Resolve` returns a promise. A resolve takes about a
  microsecond where the synchronous containers take a tenth of that or less; the
  [comparison](./reference/comparison.md#benchmarks) has the numbers. That rarely matters for an
  application, but code that must resolve synchronously can't use it.
- **Wiring is explicit.** Each class lists its `Deps`. The compiler checks them against the
  constructor, and `Validate()` checks the whole graph, but it is more code than auto-wiring.
- **Some advanced features are left out on purpose:** property injection, contextual bindings and
  auto-registration by scanning files.

## Adopting it safely

1. **Pin to the major version** (`^1` on npm or JSR), and read the changelog when you take a minor
   release.
2. **Validate the wiring in a test**, so a broken graph fails CI rather than a deploy:

   ```ts ignore
   // A fragment from a test file: build the app's container the way main.ts does, then check it.
   Deno.test('the container is wired correctly', () => {
     const app = buildContainer();

     app.Validate(); // throws IoCValidationError listing every problem
   });
   ```

3. **Start with one bounded service,** where async initialization and clean shutdown matter most,
   then expand.
4. **Check our claims yourself:** `deno task compare` re-runs the comparison, and every
   [guarantee](./reference/guarantees.md) links to its test.

## What's Next

- Five short steps from a first container to tests: [getting started](./getting-started/README.md)
  _[Tutorial]_
- What the container promises, with proof: [guarantees](./reference/guarantees.md) _[Reference]_
- What may change between releases: [versioning and support policy](./policy.md) _[Reference]_

# Comparison with other DI containers

This page is generated by `deno task compare` from the code in [`compare/`](../../compare/run.ts):
the same scenarios and the same small service graph in each library, at pinned versions. Re-run
it to check any result. Generated 2026-11-01 on Deno/2.9.6 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz.

| Library     | Package               |
| ----------- | --------------------- |
| @fathym/ioc | `this repository`     |
| InversifyJS | `npm:inversify@8.2.3` |
| awilix      | `npm:awilix@13.0.5`   |
| tsyringe    | `npm:tsyringe@4.10.0` |

Each adapter uses the library the way its documentation recommends, without decorator syntax
(InversifyJS through `toDynamicValue` and `toResolvedValue`, tsyringe by calling `injectable()`
and `inject()` directly), so the suite needs no compiler flags. That changes how dependencies are
declared, not the behavior measured. Corrections are welcome: open an issue or a pull request
against the adapter.

## Lifecycle and wiring

|                                                                |      @fathym/ioc      |                        InversifyJS                         |                            awilix                            |                           tsyringe                           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------: | :--------------------------------------------------------: | :----------------------------------------------------------: | :----------------------------------------------------------: |
| Concurrent first resolves build an async singleton once        |           ✓           |                             ✓                              |                     ✓ the cached promise                     |                     ✓ the cached promise                     |
| An async dependency is injected as the instance, not a promise |           ✓           |                        ✓ `getAsync`                        |                ✗ injects the pending promise                 |                ✗ injects the pending promise                 |
| A failed async build is retried, not cached                    |           ✓           |                  ✗ the failure is cached                   |               ✗ the rejected promise is cached               |               ✗ the rejected promise is cached               |
| A request scope disposes its instances when the request throws | ✓ `await using` scope | ✓ child container + `onDeactivation`, unbound in `finally` |               ✓ `scope.dispose()` in `finally`               |         ✓ child container, `dispose()` in `finally`          |
| Disposal runs in reverse creation order                        |           ✓           |   ✗ A, B: follows registration order, not creation order   | ✗ A, B: a dependency is disposed before the service using it | ✗ A, B: a dependency is disposed before the service using it |
| A missing dependency is found at startup, before any resolve   |    ✓ `Validate()`     |        ✗ no validation API; fails at first resolve         |         ✗ no validation API; fails at first resolve          |         ✗ no validation API; fails at first resolve          |
| A wrong dependency fails to compile                            |           ✓           |                             ✓                              |                              ✗                               |                              ✗                               |

What each row does is in [`compare/scenarios.ts`](../../compare/scenarios.ts), and how each library
does it is in [`compare/adapters/`](../../compare/adapters/ioc.ts). The compile check wires a logger
where a repository needs a database and asks whether `deno check` rejects it.

## Benchmarks

The same graph in each library: two values, a singleton repository, a transient handler, and a
scoped request context. `Resolve` in `@fathym/ioc` always returns a promise, so each resolve
includes at least one `await`; services whose dependencies are ready are built synchronously
inside it, and only work that is still pending gets a `PendingTimeoutMs` timer. The other three
resolve synchronously. Treat these as orders of magnitude on one machine, not as a ranking: at
about a microsecond per resolve, the container is rarely what limits an application.

**cold start**

| Library     | Time per iteration | Per second |
| ----------- | -----------------: | ---------: |
| tsyringe    |             1.2 µs |    838,223 |
| @fathym/ioc |            18.1 µs |     55,386 |
| awilix      |            18.6 µs |     53,818 |
| InversifyJS |            50.7 µs |     19,732 |

**resolve**

| Library     | Time per iteration | Per second |
| ----------- | -----------------: | ---------: |
| InversifyJS |              51 ns | 19,665,279 |
| awilix      |             134 ns |  7,488,224 |
| tsyringe    |             180 ns |  5,542,185 |
| @fathym/ioc |             1.2 µs |    817,166 |

**scope per request**

| Library     | Time per iteration | Per second |
| ----------- | -----------------: | ---------: |
| tsyringe    |             4.8 µs |    207,008 |
| awilix      |            17.4 µs |     57,394 |
| @fathym/ioc |            25.7 µs |     38,961 |
| InversifyJS |            72.3 µs |     13,839 |

Source: [`compare/bench.ts`](../../compare/bench.ts).

## What this page doesn't cover

- **Features we leave out on purpose:** synchronous resolution, auto-registration by scanning
  files, property injection, and contextual bindings. See
  [the README](../../README.md#how-it-compares) for when to choose another library.
- **NestJS**, which is a framework with DI built in rather than a container library.

  _[Reference]_
- Every method and option: [api.md](./api.md) _[Reference]_

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/reference/guarantees.md (Guarantees)

# Guarantees

These are the behaviors you can build on. Each one is a sentence, followed by the tests that prove
it. Links of the form _file › step_ name a test step, and the docs check fails if that step is
renamed or removed, so a guarantee can't outlive its proof. Changing any of them is a breaking
change under the [versioning policy](../policy.md#what-counts-as-breaking).

Coverage of `src/` is reported by `deno task coverage` on every push: lines 98.8%, branches 97.1%,
functions 99% (November 2026), with CI failing below 97% of lines or 95% of branches.

## Building

- **Concurrent first resolves of a singleton or scoped service build it once.** Every caller gets
  the same instance.
  - [lazy › concurrent resolves share one async creation](../../tests/ioc/lazy.tests.ts)
  - [eager-retry › a successful async singleton is built once by Activate()](../../tests/ioc/eager-retry.tests.ts)
  - [edge-cases › a factory returning a thenable builds once and is disposed](../../tests/ioc/edge-cases.tests.ts)
- **A failed build isn't cached.** The next resolve runs the factory again, whether it threw or
  rejected, and callers waiting on the failing build all get the error.
  - [lazy › a rejected creation is not memoized; the next resolve retries](../../tests/ioc/lazy.tests.ts)
  - [lazy › concurrent resolves during a failing creation all reject, then retry once](../../tests/ioc/lazy.tests.ts)
  - [lazy › a synchronous throw in a factory rejects and retries](../../tests/ioc/lazy.tests.ts)
  - [eager-retry › a resolve after a failed Activate() retries the factory](../../tests/ioc/eager-retry.tests.ts)
- **A dependency cycle throws, naming the path, instead of hanging.** That includes cycles through
  a factory's `ioc` argument.
  - [cycles › A -> B -> A through factory parameters](../../tests/ioc/cycles.tests.ts)
  - [cycles › long cycle reports the full path](../../tests/ioc/cycles.tests.ts)
  - [cycles › a failed cycle leaves services resolvable once the cycle is broken](../../tests/ioc/cycles.tests.ts)
  - [cycles › diamond dependencies resolve and share the bottom singleton](../../tests/ioc/cycles.tests.ts)

## Ownership and disposal

- **The container owns only what it built successfully.** If a factory opens something and then
  throws, cleaning that up is the factory's job. Dependencies that were built before a sibling
  failed are still owned, and disposed with the container.
  - [guarantees › a factory that throws cleans up after itself: the container owns only what was built](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)
  - [guarantees › dependencies built before a sibling failed are still disposed with the container](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)

  ```ts
  import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

  class Connection {
    static open() {
      return new Connection();
    }

    async handshake() {}

    async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {}
  }

  const ioc = new IoCContainer().RegisterFactory(Connection, async () => {
    const conn = Connection.open();

    try {
      await conn.handshake();
      return conn; // from here on, the container owns it
    } catch (err) {
      await conn[Symbol.asyncDispose](); // the factory closes what it opened
      throw err;
    }
  });

  await ioc.Resolve(Connection);
  await ioc.Dispose();
  ```

- **Each instance is disposed once, by the container or scope that built it.** Values you register
  are never disposed unless you pass a `Dispose` option, and transients are never disposed.
  - [ownership › an alias factory returning another registration: disposed once](../../tests/ioc/ownership.tests.ts)
  - [ownership › a scope resolving the root's singleton: only the root disposes it](../../tests/ioc/ownership.tests.ts)
  - [explicit › values are never disposed by the container](../../tests/ioc/explicit.tests.ts)
  - [explicit › a value given a Dispose callback is disposed with the container](../../tests/ioc/explicit.tests.ts)
  - [scopes › transients are never disposed](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [scopes › a disposed scope rejects further use; Dispose is idempotent](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
- **Instances are disposed in reverse creation order.**
  - [scopes › instances are disposed in reverse creation order](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
- **A scope disposes its instances when the request ends, including when the request throws.** If a
  disposer throws too, the caller gets a `SuppressedError` that carries both errors.
  - [scopes › await using disposes the scope instances](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [guarantees › a scope disposes its instances when the request throws](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)
  - [guarantees › when the request and a disposer both throw, the caller gets both (SuppressedError)](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)
- **Disposing a parent disposes its live scopes first, deepest first, then its own instances.** A
  scope of a disposed parent rejects every use.
  - [scopes › disposing a parent disposes its live scopes too](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [scopes › after stopping modules, live scopes are disposed deepest first, then own instances](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [scopes › a scope of a disposed parent rejects every use](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
- **One failing disposer or `OnStop` doesn't stop the rest.** Every step runs, and the failures are
  thrown together as one `IoCDisposeError` (an `AggregateError`). The one exception: a disposer
  that fails on an instance that arrived after `Dispose()` has no caller left to throw to, so its
  error is dropped.
  - [scopes › disposal errors are aggregated and every instance is still disposed](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [scopes › errors from disposing child scopes reach the parent Dispose](../../tests/ioc/scopes.tests.ts)
  - [modules › every step runs; failures are thrown together](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [ownership › a late arrival that fails to dispose is not thrown](../../tests/ioc/ownership.tests.ts)
- **`Dispose()` doesn't wait for builds in flight.** A singleton or scoped instance that finishes
  after `Dispose()` is disposed on arrival, and the waiting `Resolve` rejects with
  `IoCContainerDisposedError`. A transient that finishes later is returned to its caller, who owns
  it.
  - [ownership › an instance that finishes building after Dispose() is disposed on arrival, and the resolve rejects](../../tests/ioc/ownership.tests.ts)
  - [edge-cases › a scoped build landing after the parent is disposed is disposed](../../tests/ioc/edge-cases.tests.ts)
  - [guarantees › a transient that finishes building after Dispose() is returned to its caller, who owns it](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)

## Startup

- **`Start()` validates, then starts modules one at a time in dependency order.** If one fails, the
  started ones are stopped in reverse, and `Start()` can be called again. `Dispose()` during
  `Start()` lets the module that is starting finish, then stops it.
  - [modules › validates first, unless told not to](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [modules › runs OnStart in order, once, and reports State](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [modules › a failing OnStart stops the started modules in reverse, and can be retried](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [modules › Dispose() during Start() lets the current module finish, then stops it](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
- **`Activate()` builds every singleton, reports every failure by name, and can be retried.**
  - [eager-retry › Activate() rejects with every failure, named](../../tests/ioc/eager-retry.tests.ts)
  - [eager-retry › Activate() can be retried after a failure](../../tests/ioc/eager-retry.tests.ts)

## Timeouts and cancellation

- **`PendingTimeoutMs` (default 30 seconds) bounds every `Resolve`, every `Activate()` build, and
  each `OnStart`, `OnStop` and disposer.** `0` turns it off.
  - [modules › bounds OnStart](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [modules › bounds OnStop and disposers](../../tests/ioc/modules.tests.ts)
  - [guarantees › PendingTimeoutMs: 0 turns the timeout off](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)
- **A timeout rejects the caller; it doesn't cancel the build.** The build keeps running, and if
  it succeeds its result is cached, so the factory isn't called again.
  - [guarantees › after a timeout the build keeps running, and its late result is cached](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)
- **There is no cancellation.** The container doesn't pass an `AbortSignal` to factories. A factory
  that needs one uses its own, such as `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`.

## What `Validate()` can see

`Validate()` walks the declared dependency graph without building anything. It reports
`missing`, `cycle`, `captive` and `arguments` problems, all at once.

| Wiring                                                | Checked? | Proof                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Deps` on `RegisterClass` and `RegisterFactory`       | Yes      | [records › Validate sees factory Deps (missing, cycles, captive)](../../tests/ioc/records.tests.ts)                                  |
| A class with constructor parameters but no `Deps`     | Yes      | [validate › arguments: a class without Deps whose constructor takes parameters](../../tests/ioc/validate.tests.ts)                   |
| Registrations made by modules (`Use`)                 | Yes      | [guarantees › module registrations are validated like any other](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)                                |
| A parent singleton's dependencies, from a scope       | Yes      | [validate › a parent's singleton is checked where it is built, not in the scope](../../tests/ioc/validate.tests.ts)                  |
| Keys a factory resolves through `ioc` inside its body | No       | [validate › factories without Deps are not checked](../../tests/ioc/validate.tests.ts): declare them in `Deps`                       |
| Registrations added after `Validate()` ran            | Next run | [guarantees › Validate checks what is registered when it runs; call it again after adding more](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts) |
| A service replaced with `Override()`                  | No       | [guarantees › an Override is a value, so the overridden registration is no longer checked](../../tests/ioc/guarantees.tests.ts)      |

So: declare `Deps` on factories too, and call `Validate()` (or `Start()`, which calls it) after the
last registration.

## Compile time

- **`Deps` is checked against the constructor.** A dependency in the wrong order, missing, extra,
  or of the wrong type is a compile error, so changing a constructor without updating its `Deps`
  doesn't compile. A class registered with no `Deps` at all compiles, and `Validate()` reports it
  as an `arguments` problem instead.
  - [types › Types](../../tests/ioc/types.tests.ts)
  - [typed › the constructor parameter types are still checked](../../tests/ioc/typed.tests.ts)

## What's Next

- Every error message, its cause and the fix: [errors.md](./errors.md) _[Reference]_
- What may change between releases: [versioning and support policy](../policy.md) _[Reference]_

# Getting Started

In about fifteen minutes you'll build a small **notes API** on `Deno.serve`. Along the way you'll
learn what you need for most apps:

- **registering services** (classes, factories, values);
- **resolving** them;
- **async services** such as Deno KV, checked and built at startup;
- **giving each HTTP request its own scope**;
- **packaging the app as a module** and **swapping a dependency in a test**.

Each step introduces one idea with a small notes app, and every code block is a complete program
you can run. The steps share names (`NotesStore`, `Clock`), but each program stands on its own;
[`examples/per-request-server.ts`](../../examples/per-request-server.ts) puts them together.

> **Note:** You need [Deno](https://deno.com) 2.x. Steps 3 and 5 use Deno KV, so run them with
> `--unstable-kv`; step 4 runs a server, so it needs `--allow-net`.

| Step | Document                                                      | You'll learn                                                           |
| ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | [installation.md](./installation.md) _[Tutorial]_             | Add the package and import it                                          |
| 2    | [first-container.md](./first-container.md) _[Tutorial]_       | Register and resolve classes, factories, values and typed tokens       |
| 3    | [async-services.md](./async-services.md) _[Tutorial]_         | Open Deno KV from an async factory, check the wiring, build it at boot |
| 4    | [per-request-scopes.md](./per-request-scopes.md) _[Tutorial]_ | Give every HTTP request its own scope                                  |
| 5    | [testing-your-app.md](./testing-your-app.md) _[Tutorial]_     | Put the wiring in a module, and swap the store for a fake in a test    |

When you're done, the [API reference](../reference/api.md) lists every method and option, the
[error catalog](../reference/errors.md) explains every error message, and the
[examples](../../examples/README.md) are small programs you can run and copy.

Start with [step 1: installation](./installation.md).

---

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/getting-started/installation.md (Step 1: Installation)

# Step 1: Installation

> **Goal:** Add the container to your project and confirm the import works.

## Deno

```sh
deno add jsr:@fathym/ioc
```

This adds an entry to your `deno.json` import map:

```jsonc
{
  "imports": {
    "@fathym/ioc": "jsr:@fathym/ioc@^1.0.0"
  }
}
```

## Node.js and Bun

The package is published on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fathym/ioc):

```sh
npm install @fathym/ioc         # npm
bun add @fathym/ioc             # Bun
pnpm add @fathym/ioc            # pnpm
yarn add @fathym/ioc            # Yarn
```

Every stable release is published to npm and [JSR](https://jsr.io/@fathym/ioc) with the same
version, so you can also install it from JSR (`npx jsr add @fathym/ioc`,
`bunx jsr add @fathym/ioc`, `pnpm add jsr:@fathym/ioc`).

You import it as `@fathym/ioc` either way. It is plain ESM with no runtime dependencies, and it
imports no Deno, Node.js or browser modules.

## Requirements

| What                    | Supported                                         | Checked in CI                                   |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Deno                    | 2.x                                               | the full test suite                             |
| Node.js                 | 20 and later                                      | a smoke test on 20, 22 and 24                   |
| Bun                     | 1.x                                               | a smoke test                                    |
| TypeScript              | 5.4 and later                                     | a consumer type-checked with 5.4 and the latest |
| Browsers, workers, edge | any runtime with ES2022 and `Symbol.asyncDispose` | not yet                                         |

**TypeScript settings.** The types use `Symbol.asyncDispose`, so your `lib` needs
`esnext.disposable` (or `esnext`), or turn on `skipLibCheck` (most project templates do). Using
`await using` in your own code needs that `lib` anyway:

```jsonc
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022", "ESNext.Disposable"]
  }
}
```

> **Note:** A class key is the class itself, so minifying class names never changes which
> service you get. Errors and `Describe()` print class names, though: keep them readable with
> `keepNames: true` in esbuild and Vite (`keep_classnames: true` in Terser).

**Runtimes without explicit resource management.** `await using` needs runtime support (or a
compiler that down-levels it). Without it, call `await scope.Dispose()` yourself.

## Check it works

Create `main.ts`:

```ts
import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class Greeter {
  public greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}!`;
  }
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer();

ioc.RegisterClass(Greeter);

const greeter = await ioc.Resolve(Greeter);

console.log(greeter.greet('IoC'));
```

Run it:

```sh
deno run main.ts
# Hello, IoC!
```

That's the whole loop: **register** a service, then **resolve** it. The container builds the
`Greeter` for you and hands back the same instance every time you ask, because services are
singletons unless you say otherwise.

## What's Next

- Register classes, factories and values, and meet typed tokens:
  [first-container.md](./first-container.md) _[Tutorial]_
- Every registration method and option: [api.md](../reference/api.md) _[Reference]_

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/getting-started/first-container.md (Step 2: Your First Container)

# Step 2: Your First Container

> **Goal:** Wire up the core of the notes app. You'll register services three different ways and
> resolve them without writing a single `new` for the app's objects.

## What you'll build

A `NotesService` that stamps each note with the time from a `Clock`, plus the app's name as a
plain value.

## Register and resolve

```ts
import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

// A typed token: a key that carries the type of what's registered under it.
const $AppName = IoCToken<string, 'AppName'>('AppName');

class Clock {
  public now(): Date {
    return new Date();
  }
}

class NotesService {
  readonly #notes: string[] = [];

  constructor(private clock: Clock) {}

  public add(text: string): string {
    const note = `${this.clock.now().toISOString()} ${text}`;
    this.#notes.push(note);
    return note;
  }

  public list(): string[] {
    return [...this.#notes];
  }
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer();

ioc.RegisterValue($AppName, 'Notes'); // 1. a value you already have
ioc.RegisterClass(Clock); // 2. a class the container constructs
ioc.RegisterFactory(NotesService, async (c) => new NotesService(await c.Resolve(Clock))); // 3. a factory

const notes = await ioc.Resolve(NotesService);

notes.add('Buy milk');

console.log(await ioc.Resolve($AppName), notes.list());
// Notes [ "2026-10-13T12:00:00.000Z Buy milk" ]
```

Three things to notice:

1. **`Resolve($AppName)` returns a `string`.** The token carries the type, so there is no generic
   to write and nothing to cast.
2. **The factory receives the container (`c`).** Resolve dependencies through that parameter,
   not through a captured `ioc`. It's what makes scopes, overrides and immediate cycle detection
   work later.
3. **You never called `new Clock()`.** The container did.

> **Note:** A token is its name: `IoCToken('AppName')` is `Symbol.for('AppName')`, so every call
> with the same name, in any package, gives the same key. Pick names that won't collide with other
> packages (`'notes/AppName'`), declare each token once, and import it wherever you need it. A
> class key is the class itself, so two different classes named `Clock` are two different keys.

## Let the container call the constructor

Writing a factory just to pass dependencies along gets repetitive. Declare the dependencies
instead, and the container checks them against the constructor's parameters at compile time:

```ts
import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class Clock {
  public now(): Date {
    return new Date();
  }
}

class NotesService {
  constructor(public clock: Clock) {}
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer();

ioc.RegisterClass(Clock);
ioc.RegisterClass(NotesService, { Deps: [Clock] }); // a type error if NotesService's constructor changes

const notes = await ioc.Resolve(NotesService);

console.log(notes.clock instanceof Clock); // true
```

## Catch missing registrations at compile time

`Deps` checks types, but on its own it can't tell whether `Clock` was registered at all. Make the
container **typed** and chain the registrations. Then `Deps` may only name what's registered
above it:

```ts
import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

const $AppName = IoCToken<string, 'AppName'>('AppName');

class Clock {
  public now(): Date {
    return new Date();
  }
}

class NotesService {
  constructor(public clock: Clock, public appName: string) {}
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer()
  .Typed()
  .RegisterValue($AppName, 'Notes')
  .RegisterClass(Clock)
  .RegisterClass(NotesService, { Deps: [Clock, $AppName] });

const notes = await ioc.Resolve(NotesService);

console.log(notes.appName); // Notes
```

Move `.RegisterClass(Clock)` below `NotesService` and the code no longer compiles. The error names
what is registered so far, so you know what to move. Typed containers are optional; later steps
use them where they help.

## Same instance, or a new one?

By default every service is a **singleton**: built once and shared. Ask for a **transient**
lifetime when you want a fresh instance on every resolve:

```ts
import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class Draft {
  public text = '';
}

class Clock {}

const ioc = new IoCContainer();

ioc.RegisterClass(Clock); // singleton (the default)
ioc.RegisterClass(Draft, { Lifetime: 'transient' });

console.log((await ioc.Resolve(Clock)) === (await ioc.Resolve(Clock))); // true
console.log((await ioc.Resolve(Draft)) === (await ioc.Resolve(Draft))); // false
```

There's a third lifetime, `scoped`, which you'll use in [step 4](./per-request-scopes.md).

## What's Next

- Start an async service (Deno KV) and check the wiring at startup:
  [async-services.md](./async-services.md) _[Tutorial]_
- Every registration option and lifetime: [api.md](../reference/api.md) _[Reference]_

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/getting-started/async-services.md (Step 3: Async Services)

# Step 3: Async Services

> **Goal:** Store notes in Deno KV. Opening a database is asynchronous, which is exactly what this
> container is built for.

## Register an async factory

```ts
import { IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class NotesStore {
  constructor(private kv: Deno.Kv) {}

  public async add(text: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.kv.set(['notes', crypto.randomUUID()], text);
  }

  public async list(): Promise<string[]> {
    const notes: string[] = [];

    for await (const entry of this.kv.list<string>({ prefix: ['notes'] })) {
      notes.push(entry.value);
    }

    return notes;
  }
}

await using ioc = new IoCContainer() // disposed (KV closed) at the end of the program
  .Typed()
  // Deno.Kv is a class, so it works as a key. The factory is async; that's fine.
  .RegisterFactory(Deno.Kv, () => Deno.openKv(':memory:'))
  .RegisterClass(NotesStore, { Deps: [Deno.Kv] });

await ioc.Start(); // checks the wiring; builds nothing
await ioc.Activate(); // opens KV now, so a bad connection fails at startup

const store = await ioc.Resolve(NotesStore);

await store.add('Buy milk');

console.log(await store.list()); // [ "Buy milk" ]
```

Run it with `deno run --unstable-kv main.ts`.

## What just happened

- **Nothing is built at registration.** A singleton is built the first time something needs it.
- **`Start()` checks the wiring.** It runs `Validate()`, which reports every missing, cyclic or
  captive dependency at once, then starts the app's modules (you'll write one in step 5). It
  doesn't build services.
- **`Activate()` builds every singleton now.** It reports all failures together in one
  `IoCActivationError`. That's how you get lazy registration _and_ fail-fast startup.
- **Concurrent resolves share one creation.** If ten requests resolve `NotesStore` at the same
  moment, KV is still opened once.
- **A failed creation is retried, not cached.** If KV isn't reachable on the first try, the next
  resolve (or `Activate()`) tries again.
- **Disposing the container cleans up what it created.** `await using` calls `Dispose()` when
  `ioc` goes out of scope. `Deno.Kv` implements `Symbol.dispose`, so the container closes it.
  Things are disposed last created, first disposed. A value you register with `RegisterValue` is
  yours: the container doesn't dispose it unless you pass a `Dispose` option.
- **Nothing waits forever.** A resolve that is still pending after 30 seconds fails with an
  `IoCResolveTimeoutError` naming the service. `new IoCContainer({ PendingTimeoutMs })` changes
  the limit; `0` turns it off.

> **Note:** `Resolve` is always `async`, even for services that aren't. One rule, everywhere: you
> never have to know whether a dependency's setup is async.

## What's Next

- Give each HTTP request its own scope: [per-request-scopes.md](./per-request-scopes.md)
  _[Tutorial]_

  [api.md](../reference/api.md) _[Reference]_

  _[Reference]_

# Step 4: Per-Request Scopes

> **Goal:** Serve the notes API over HTTP, with services that belong to a single request, such as
> the request itself and a request ID.

## Create a scope per request

```ts
import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

const $Request = IoCToken<Request, 'Request'>('Request');

class RequestContext {
  public readonly id = crypto.randomUUID();
}

class NotesHandler {
  constructor(private ctx: RequestContext, private req: Request) {}

  public handle(): Response {
    return Response.json({ requestId: this.ctx.id, path: new URL(this.req.url).pathname });
  }
}

const ioc = new IoCContainer()
  .Typed()
  .Expect($Request) // registered on each request's scope, below
  .RegisterClass(RequestContext, { Lifetime: 'scoped' })
  .RegisterClass(NotesHandler, { Deps: [RequestContext, $Request], Lifetime: 'transient' });

const server = Deno.serve({ port: 0, onListen() {} }, async (req) => {
  await using scope = ioc.CreateScope(); // disposed when the handler returns

  scope.RegisterValue($Request, req); // this request only

  return (await scope.Resolve(NotesHandler)).handle();
});

const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${server.addr.port}/notes`);

console.log(await res.json()); // { requestId: "…", path: "/notes" }

await server.shutdown();
```

Run it with `deno run --allow-net main.ts`.

## What just happened

- **`CreateScope()` makes a cheap child container.** It can resolve everything the root can.
  Nothing is copied. A scope that owns something to dispose (a disposable scoped instance) is
  tracked by the root, so even a forgotten scope is closed when the root is disposed. This one
  owns nothing to dispose, so it isn't tracked at all.
- **`scoped` services get one instance per scope.** Every service in this request shares the same
  `RequestContext`; the next request gets a new one.
- **Registrations on a scope stay in that scope.** `$Request` exists only inside this request's
  scope. `Expect($Request)` tells the typed container it will be there, so `Deps` may name it,
  and `Validate()` counts it as registered. A scope may also register a key the root already has;
  its registration wins inside the scope.
- **Transient services built in a scope receive the scope.** That's how `NotesHandler` sees this
  request's `$Request` and `RequestContext`.
- **`await using` disposes the scope** when the handler finishes, disposing the scoped instances
  it built.

> **Warning:** A scope is a child container _you_ create. It is not tied to an HTTP request
> unless you create one per request, as above. A singleton is built once, by the container it is
> registered in, and shared by every scope. Resolving a `scoped` service from the root throws
> `IoCScopeRequiredError`, and `Validate()` reports a singleton that depends on a scoped service
> (a `captive`), so one request's data can't leak into a shared instance.

## What's Next

- Swap the store for a fake in a test: [testing-your-app.md](./testing-your-app.md) _[Tutorial]_
- `CreateScope()`, `Isolate()` and lifetimes in full: [api.md](../reference/api.md) _[Reference]_
- A complete server with a scope per request and graceful shutdown:
  [examples/per-request-server.ts](../../examples/per-request-server.ts) _[Example]_

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/getting-started/testing-your-app.md (Step 5: Testing Your App)

# Step 5: Testing Your App

> **Goal:** Package the app's wiring as a module, then test `NotesService` without a real
> database by swapping the store for a fake.

Deno doesn't support Jest-style module mocking. That's fine: the container _is_ the seam. Put the
real wiring in a module, add it to a test container, and override the one service you want to
fake.

## Put the wiring in a module

A module is a named set of registrations, with optional `OnStart` and `OnStop` hooks. Its
`Register`, `OnStart` and `OnStop` each receive the container. `main.ts` and the tests both add
the same module with `Use()`:

```ts
import { DefineModule, IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

class NotesService {
  public list(): string[] {
    return [];
  }
}

// notes-app.ts: the app's real wiring.
const NotesApp = DefineModule({
  Name: 'NotesApp',
  Register: (ioc) => ioc.RegisterClass(NotesService),
  OnStart: () => console.log('notes ready'),
  OnStop: () => console.log('notes stopped'),
});

// main.ts
await using ioc = new IoCContainer().Use(NotesApp);

await ioc.Start(); // validates the wiring, then runs OnStart: notes ready

console.log((await ioc.Resolve(NotesService)).list()); // []

// At the end of the program, `await using` disposes the container: notes stopped
```

## Override a dependency in a test

```ts
import { assertEquals } from 'jsr:@std/assert@1.0.16';
import { DefineModule, IoCContainer } from '@fathym/ioc';

// The abstract class is the key; the app and the test provide different implementations.
abstract class NotesStore {
  public abstract add(text: string): Promise<void>;
  public abstract list(): Promise<string[]>;
}

class KvNotesStore extends NotesStore {
  constructor(private kv: Deno.Kv) {
    super();
  }

  public async add(text: string) {
    await this.kv.set(['notes', crypto.randomUUID()], text);
  }

  public async list() {
    const notes: string[] = [];
    for await (const e of this.kv.list<string>({ prefix: ['notes'] })) notes.push(e.value);
    return notes;
  }
}

class NotesService {
  constructor(private store: NotesStore) {}

  public async addNote(text: string): Promise<string[]> {
    await this.store.add(text.trim());
    return await this.store.list();
  }
}

// The app's real wiring, shared by main.ts and the tests.
const NotesApp = DefineModule({
  Name: 'NotesApp',
  Register: (ioc) =>
    ioc
      .RegisterFactory(Deno.Kv, () => Deno.openKv(':memory:'))
      .RegisterFactory(NotesStore, (_ioc, kv) => new KvNotesStore(kv), { Deps: [Deno.Kv] })
      .RegisterClass(NotesService, { Deps: [NotesStore] }),
});

Deno.test('the real wiring is valid', () => {
  new IoCContainer().Use(NotesApp).Validate(); // throws IoCValidationError if anything is missing
});

Deno.test('NotesService trims notes before saving', async () => {
  await using ioc = new IoCContainer().Use(NotesApp);

  const saved: string[] = [];

  ioc.Override(NotesStore, {
    add: (text) => Promise.resolve(void saved.push(text)),
    list: () => Promise.resolve(saved),
  });

  const service = await ioc.Resolve(NotesService);

  assertEquals(await service.addNote('  Buy milk  '), ['Buy milk']);
});
```

Run it with `deno test --unstable-kv`.

## Why this works

- **The test uses the real wiring** (`NotesApp`), so the first test also proves the registrations
  are right.
- **`Override()` works on any container.** It replaces the registration with a value and returns
  a function that puts back exactly what was there before. Use that function when a container is
  shared across tests; here each test makes its own, and `await using` disposes it when the test
  ends.
- **Override before you resolve.** `NotesService` is a singleton; it is built on the first
  `Resolve`, after the override, so it receives the fake. An instance built earlier keeps what it
  was given.
- **The real KV store is never opened.** Nothing is built at registration, and nothing resolves
  it.

> **Note:** You can also register a fake on a scope (`ioc.CreateScope().RegisterValue(...)`),
> which leaves the container itself untouched. Scope registrations reach **transient and scoped**
> services resolved from the scope; a singleton is built by the container it was registered in.

## You're done

You've used most of what you'll need day to day:

- **registration:** classes, factories, values and tokens;
- **lifetimes:** singleton, transient and scoped;
- **async startup** with `Start()` and `Activate()`;
- **per-request scopes** with disposal;
- **modules** that package the wiring, with start and stop hooks;
- **test overrides** with `Override()`.

# Working with AI coding agents

> **Goal:** have an AI coding agent write and change `@fathym/ioc` wiring correctly the first
> time, and fix it on its own when it doesn't.

`@fathym/ioc` keeps the wiring explicit: every registration and every `Deps` list is in the code,
checked by the compiler, and checked again by `Validate()`. That gives an agent something it can
read and a loop it can follow. Three things make the most of it.

## 1. Install the agent kit

The kit is the library's conventions written for agents, as each tool's instruction file:

```sh
deno run -A jsr:@fathym/ioc/init-agents
```

It writes:

| File                                 | Read by                           |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| `.claude/skills/fathym-ioc/SKILL.md` | Claude Code (as a skill)          |
| `.cursor/rules/fathym-ioc.mdc`       | Cursor                            |
| `AGENTS.md` (a marked section)       | Codex and other `AGENTS.md` tools |
| `.github/copilot-instructions.md`    | GitHub Copilot                    |

Pick some with `--targets=claude,agents-md`. Running it again updates the `@fathym/ioc` section
of `AGENTS.md` and the Copilot file without touching the rest. From Node.js or Bun, call
`writeAgentKit()` from `@fathym/ioc/agents`, or read the rules as text from `IOC_AGENT_RULES`.

## 2. Point the agent at the full docs

[`llms-full.txt`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/llms-full.txt) holds every docs
page and example program in one file, and [`llms.txt`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/llms.txt)
is its index. Every code example in both is type-checked and run in CI, so an agent that reads
them copies code that works.

## 3. Let it use the fix loop

The kit teaches this loop; it works because each step returns something an agent can act on:

1. **The compiler** rejects `Deps` that don't match the constructor (order, count or type).
2. **`Validate()`** lists every wiring problem at once, each with a `Fix:` line:

   ```ts
   import { IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

   class Repo {
     constructor(public url: string) {}
   }

   const $Url = IoCToken<string, 'app/Url'>('app/Url');

   const issues = new IoCContainer().RegisterClass(Repo, { Deps: [$Url] }).Validate({
     Throw: false,
   });

   console.log(issues[0].Hint); // Register app/Url with RegisterClass, RegisterFactory or RegisterValue, …
   ```

3. **Runtime errors** have a stable `code` and a `DocsUrl` that opens the code's section of the
   [error catalog](../reference/errors.md#error-codes), with the cause and the fix.

Keep a test that builds the container and calls `Validate()`, so the agent finds wiring mistakes
by running the tests, not by running the app.

## What's Next

- The conventions in full: [`src/agents/rules.ts`](../../src/agents/rules.ts) _[Reference]_
- Every error code and its fix: [errors.md](../reference/errors.md#error-codes) _[Reference]_
- Every guide: [guides](./README.md) _[How-to]_

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fathym/ioc/main/docs/guides/registering-many-modules.md (Registering many modules)

# Registering many modules

> **Goal:** register every module in a folder with one call, and keep adding modules without
> touching the app's startup code.

Some containers scan the file system and register whatever they find by naming convention. That
needs file-system access at startup and a glob library, and it hides the wiring. With
@fathym/ioc, a module already carries its own registrations and lifecycle, so all you need is one
list of modules. Two ways to keep that list:

## A barrel file

Give the folder one file that lists its modules. Adding a module is one line there:

```ts ignore
// modules/mod.ts: a fragment showing the barrel file itself.
import { Database } from './database.ts';
import { Mailer } from './mailer.ts';
import { Api } from './api.ts';

export const AppModules = [Database, Mailer, Api] as const;
```

The app then adds them all at once. `Use()` also adds each module's `Requires` for you, and
`Start()` starts them in dependency order, so the order in the list doesn't matter:

```ts
import { DefineModule, IoCContainer, IoCToken } from '@fathym/ioc';

interface Db {
  query(sql: string): Promise<string[]>;
}

const $Db = IoCToken<Db, 'app/Db'>('app/Db');

// These three would live in modules/database.ts, modules/mailer.ts and modules/api.ts.
const Database = DefineModule({
  Name: 'Database',
  Register: (ioc) => ioc.RegisterValue($Db, { query: async () => ['ada'] }),
  OnStart: () => console.log('database connected'),
});

const Mailer = DefineModule({
  Name: 'Mailer',
  Register: (ioc) => ioc,
  OnStart: () => console.log('mailer ready'),
});

const Api = DefineModule({
  Name: 'Api',
  Requires: [Database],
  Register: (ioc) => ioc,
  OnStart: () => console.log('api listening'),
});

// modules/mod.ts
const AppModules = [Api, Mailer, Database] as const;

// main.ts
await using app = new IoCContainer().Use(...AppModules);

await app.Start(); // database connected, api listening, mailer ready

console.log(await (await app.Resolve($Db)).query('select name from users')); // ['ada']
```

Keeping the list `as const` keeps the types: on a [typed container](../reference/api.md#typed),
`Use(...AppModules)` checks every module's `Needs` and adds what each one provides.

## `import.meta.glob` under Vite

Vite (and Vitest) can collect a folder at build time, so new files are picked up without editing a
list. Every export that looks like a module is added:

```ts ignore
// A fragment: import.meta.glob is provided by Vite, not by Deno, Node.js or Bun.
import { IoCContainer, type IoCModule } from '@fathym/ioc';

const files = import.meta.glob<Record<string, unknown>>('./modules/*.ts', { eager: true });

const isModule = (value: unknown): value is IoCModule =>
  typeof (value as IoCModule)?.Name === 'string' &&
  typeof (value as IoCModule)?.Register === 'function';

const modules = Object.values(files).flatMap((file) => Object.values(file).filter(isModule));

await using app = new IoCContainer().Use(...modules);

await app.Start();
```

The glob version gives up the compile-time `Needs` check, because the list is only known when
the bundle is built. `Start()` still validates the wiring and fails with every problem listed.

# API Reference

Everything is exported from `@fathym/ioc`. The generated docs on
[JSR](https://jsr.io/@fathym/ioc/doc) come from the same JSDoc and always match a release. This
page groups the API by task and adds behavior notes and examples.

Signature blocks are declarations, shown for reading (they are marked `ts ignore`). Every other
code block is a complete, runnable example, checked in CI.

**Contents:**

- **Creating:** [new IoCContainer](#new-ioccontaineroptions), [State](#state)
- **Registration:** [keys and IoCToken](#keys-and-ioctokenname),
  [RegisterClass](#registerclassclass-options),

  [Unregister](#unregisterkey-name)

- **Resolution:** [Resolve](#resolvekey-name), [TryResolve](#tryresolvekey-name),
  [ResolveAll](#resolveallkey), [ResolveNamed](#resolvenamedkey),

  [how resolution behaves](#how-resolution-behaves)
- **Scopes:** [CreateScope](#createscope), [Isolate](#isolatekeys)
- **Modules:** [Use](#usemodules), [IoCModule](#iocmodule),
  [DefineModule](#definemoduledefinition)

  [what gets disposed](#what-gets-disposed)
